Meme 101A / Level 6

LEVEL 6 OF 8

Understand Attention

Understand why people notice a meme token and how attention turns into — or fails to turn into — demand.

1. Narrative

01Definition

A narrative is the story used to explain why a token might attract buyers. Meta describes a broader theme across tokens. Alpha means a claimed information advantage; it needs verification.

02Why it matters

Meme tokens often compete for attention more than traditional fundamentals.

03What to check

  • Original announcement, date, and exact token address
  • Whether posts add new information or repeat one source
  • Actual buying and returning participation
  • Competing tokens in the same theme

04Healthy / Dangerous

Healthy

The story is supported by sources linked to the exact token.

Dangerous

A familiar name or compelling story is treated as proof of identity or demand.

05Beginner mistake

Confusing a good story with guaranteed price appreciation.

06Takeaway

Narrative creates attention; buyers still have to convert that attention into demand.

See it in Meme Fast → Tweet

Follow source evidence and confirm the exact chain and contract association; a name match alone is a lead.

2. Catalyst

01Definition

A catalyst is an event that can increase attention or demand.

Examples

  • Exchange listing
  • Product launch
  • Chain announcement
  • Major account mention
  • Community event

02Why it matters

An event can change access or participation, but an announcement alone does not establish new demand.

03What to check

  • Whether the catalyst is confirmed
  • Whether it is already priced in
  • Whether new users can actually act on it

04Healthy / Dangerous

Healthy

A primary source confirms what changes and when.

Dangerous

Rumours or an announced date are treated as guaranteed new buying.

05Beginner mistake

Buying only because a date or announcement exists.

06Takeaway

A catalyst matters only if it changes attention, access, or demand.

See it in Meme Fast → Tweet

Open the underlying source and verify the announcement with a primary source. A feed item does not confirm future demand.

3. Social Momentum

01Definition

Social momentum is the rate at which discussion and participation are growing.

02Why it matters

A meme often needs continuously expanding attention to sustain high valuations.

03What to check

  • Number of independent accounts discussing it
  • Engagement quality
  • Growth over time
  • New communities joining
  • Whether discussion survives price weakness

04Healthy / Dangerous

Healthy

Discussion broadens across independent participants and persists over time.

Dangerous

Repeated posts from a small group inflate the apparent audience.

05Beginner mistake

Counting posts without checking whether they come from the same small group.

06Takeaway

Broadening participation matters more than raw post count.

See it in Meme Fast → Tweet

Inspect indexed X mentions and their evidence. RSS counts do not measure author diversity, engagement, or all X activity.

4. CT / KOL Shilling

01Definition

Crypto Twitter or KOL shilling happens when influential accounts promote or discuss a token.

02Why it matters

Influencers can create rapid inflows, but those inflows can reverse just as quickly.

03What to check

  • When the KOL entered
  • Whether they disclosed holdings
  • Whether they are still holding
  • Whether multiple KOLs are connected
  • How late you are relative to their entry

04Healthy / Dangerous

Healthy

Separate promotional claims from source evidence and disclosed incentives.

Dangerous

Coordinated promotion coincides with early holders reducing inventory.

05Beginner mistake

Assuming a KOL mention creates permanent demand.

06Takeaway

Influence can create attention faster than liquidity can absorb exits.

See it in Meme Fast → Tweet

Review available source posts as leads. Holdings, sponsorship, and wallet attribution require independent verification.

5. Attention Rotation

01Definition

Attention rotation is the movement of trader interest from one meme, theme, chain, or sector to another.

02Why it matters

A good token can stagnate if the market's attention moves elsewhere.

03What to check

  • Which themes are gaining volume
  • Which chains are gaining meme activity
  • Whether previous leaders are losing participation
  • Whether capital is rotating into new launches

04Healthy / Dangerous

Healthy

Compare attention evidence with sampled activity across themes and chains.

Dangerous

A token is assessed in isolation as participation moves elsewhere.

05Beginner mistake

Evaluating a token without considering what the rest of the meme market is doing.

06Takeaway

Meme performance is partly relative: attention has alternatives.

See it in Meme Fast → Tweet

Compare stories and sampled activity across themes. The feed does not measure total attention or capital rotation.

6. Chain Narrative

01Definition

A chain narrative is the broader story around the blockchain where the meme trades.

02Why it matters

A chain experiencing strong user growth, new products, or speculative interest can lift its meme ecosystem.

03What to check

  • Chain activity
  • DEX volume
  • Launchpad activity
  • New users
  • Ecosystem catalysts

04Healthy / Dangerous

Healthy

Chain-level claims are checked against sources and token-specific activity.

Dangerous

A popular chain is treated as sufficient evidence for every token on it.

05Beginner mistake

Assuming every token on a hot chain will benefit equally.

06Takeaway

A strong chain can provide wind at the token's back, but it does not remove token-specific risk.

See it in Meme Fast → Tweet

Follow chain-related stories to their sources. Chain-wide user and DEX growth need separate evidence.

7. Meme Lifecycle

01Definition

An attention lifecycle is a working description of how participation changes, not a guaranteed sequence.

Common path

Emergence → Acceleration → Expansion → Maturity → Decline → Exhaustion. Extension: Maturity → Renewal → Expansion.

02Why it matters

The same chart can mean different things depending on which stage the token is in.

03What to check

  • Holder growth
  • Social growth
  • Large-wallet behavior
  • Liquidity
  • Whether new attention is still entering

04Healthy / Dangerous

Healthy

The strategy matches observed launch stage, attention, and ownership changes.

Dangerous

An early-launch playbook is applied to a mature distribution phase.

05Beginner mistake

Using an early-launch strategy on a mature token.

06Takeaway

Know what stage of the story you are trading.

See it in Meme Fast → Snipe

Start with observed launch stage, then compare story and market context. Launch stage is only one part of the lifecycle.

Level 6 Checklist

Ask:

  1. Why are people paying attention?
  2. Is the narrative growing or becoming stale?
  3. Is there a real catalyst?
  4. Is social activity broad or concentrated?
  5. Are KOLs early, late, holding, or exiting?
  6. Is attention rotating into or away from this chain or theme?

Work through the evidence

Illustrative case: Trace attention into the exact token

A news event attracts 20 indexed posts, then 40 in an equal later window. Some are reposts and several name a different contract with the same ticker. The raw count rose; exact-token independent interest may not have doubled.

Even if credible attention grows, buying can stay flat while early inventory sells. Conversely, a token can attract buying before indexed posts arrive. Compare timestamps and coverage instead of treating one metric as the cause of the other.

How to investigate it

Trace the primary story, publication date, and exact-contract association. Separate independent sources, repetitions, and aliases. Compare equivalent attention and trade windows and record indexing lag. Write what changed in interest and what changed in market participation as separate conclusions. For claimed alpha, open the primary announcement and match its date and full token address. A screenshot or repost alone does not verify an integration, launch, or partnership.

Check your reasoning — answered

Does zero RSS mentions mean no attention exists? No. It means none appeared in that bounded indexed sample. Absence from a sample is not total audience absence.
